fatNotes.title: Climate Change Science & Global Warming (W5S1, W5S2)
fatNotes.intro: Physics of the greenhouse effect, atmospheric drivers, 4 pillars of empirical evidence, causes vs natural factors, consequences, and mitigation vs adaptation.

sections.heading: 1. Greenhouse Effect Fundamentals
sections.content:
• Natural greenhouse effect = beneficial heat trapping keeping Earth's mean temperature at ~15 °C (without it: -18 °C).
• Enhanced greenhouse effect = excessive anthropogenic radiative forcing caused by elevated GHG concentrations from fossil fuel burning, deforestation, and industrial processes.
• Radiation physics: Sun emits short-wave radiation (visible, UV) which penetrates the atmosphere and heats Earth's surface. The warmed surface re-emits thermal radiation as long-wave infrared. Greenhouse gases absorb this infrared radiation and re-radiate it in all directions, trapping heat in the lower troposphere.

sections.heading: 2. Key Greenhouse Gases Table
tableRows: Fossil fuel combustion (coal, oil, gas), cement production, deforestation
Stays centuries to millennia; baseline reference (GWP = 1)
Enteric fermentation (cattle), rice paddies, landfills, fossil fuel leaks
Short-lived (~12 yrs) but 80–84x more potent than CO2 over 20 yrs (GWP100 = 28–34)
Synthetic nitrogen fertilisers, manure management, nylon/chemical industry
~114 yrs lifespan; ~265x more potent than CO2 (GWP100 = 265–298)
Natural hydrological evaporation (amplified by warming air)
Most abundant GHG by volume; acts as a powerful positive feedback amplifier
Refrigeration, AC, semiconductor manufacturing, electrical switchgear
Synthetic gases; GWPs thousands to tens of thousands; persist centuries

sections.heading: 3. Four Independent Pillars of Evidence
sections.content:
1. Rising Surface Temperatures: Global mean temp up ~1.1 °C; 19 of the 20 hottest years on record have occurred since 2000 (NASA, NOAA, UK Met Office, JMA).
2. Rising Atmospheric CO2: Surged from 280 ppm pre-industrial to >420 ppm; confirmed by Antarctic ice core bubbles dating back 800,000 years.
3. Melting Cryosphere & Sea Level Rise: Arctic summer sea ice extent shrinking ~13%/decade; Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets losing mass; global mean sea level up ~20 cm since 1900.
4. Ocean Warming & Acidification: Oceans have absorbed >90% of excess heat and 25–30% of anthropogenic CO2; dissolving CO2 forms carbonic acid (H2CO3), dropping pH by 0.1 units (~26% acidity surge).

sections.heading: 4. Why Natural Factors Do NOT Explain Warming
sections.content:
• Volcanic Eruptions: Eject sulfate aerosols into the stratosphere that reflect sunlight, causing short-term cooling (1–3 years), not warming.
• Solar Output: Satellite observations confirm solar irradiance has slightly decreased since the 1980s while Earth's surface warmed rapidly.
• Milankovitch Orbital Cycles: Operate on timescales of 20,000 to 100,000 years — incapable of driving century-scale rapid warming.

sections.heading: 5. Mitigation vs Adaptation
tableRows: Reduce or prevent greenhouse gas emissions; enhance carbon sinks
Adjust ecological, social, or economic systems to cope with unavoidable impacts
Renewable energy (solar, wind), energy efficiency, reforestation, Carbon Capture & Storage (CCS), electric vehicles
Sea walls, flood barriers, drought-resistant crop varieties, early warning systems, rainwater harvesting, elevated roadways
Global benefit with long-term atmospheric delay
Local/regional benefit with immediate protective effect

sections.heading: 6. Policy Frameworks & Indian Commitments
sections.content:
• Paris Agreement (2015): Legally binding treaty aiming to hold global warming well below 2 °C and pursue efforts to cap warming at 1.5 °C above pre-industrial baselines.
• Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs): National climate pledges updated every 5 years.
• India's NDC & Glasgow COP26 Commitments: Net-Zero by 2070; 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030; 50% cumulative electric power from non-fossil sources by 2030; carbon intensity reduction of 45% by 2030.
• National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC, 2008): 8 National Missions — Solar Mission, Enhanced Energy Efficiency, Sustainable Habitat, Water Mission, Sustaining Himalayan Ecosystem, Green India Mission (afforestation), Sustainable Agriculture, Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change.

fatNotes.title: Carbon Footprint & Mitigation Strategies (W5S3)
fatNotes.intro: Standardized GHG quantification (Scopes 1, 2, 3), Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), sectoral emission breakdowns, mitigation pillars, and carbon offsets.

sections.heading: 1. Scopes of Carbon Footprint (Greenhouse Gas Protocol)
tableRows: GHG emissions directly from owned or company-controlled sources (boilers, furnaces, company-owned vehicles, chemical reaction vessels).
Emissions from the generation of purchased electricity, steam, heating, or cooling consumed by the organization.

All other indirect emissions throughout the upstream and downstream supply chain (raw materials extraction, transport, customer product use, end-of-life disposal). Frequently accounts for >70% of a company's total footprint.

sections.heading: 2. Carbon Accounting Standards & LCA
sections.content:
• Life Cycle Assessment (LCA): Primary engineering tool assessing cumulative environmental impacts from 'cradle' (raw material extraction) to 'grave' (disposal). 'Cradle to cradle' closes the loop through repair, remanufacture, and recycling.
• Standards to Memorise:
- GHG Protocol: Most widely used global corporate accounting standard.
- ISO 14064: International standard for organizational GHG inventories and verification.
- PAS 2050: Standard specifically measuring life cycle GHG emissions of goods and services.

sections.heading: 3. Global Sectoral Breakdown
tableRows: Phase out coal (emits ~2x CO2/MWh vs natural gas); rapid buildout of solar PV, wind, hydro, and nuclear baseload.
Iron & steel (green hydrogen direct reduction), cement (clinker substitution, CCS), circular aluminium.
Methane capture from manure, precision nitrogen fertilisation, agroforestry, alternate wetting/drying in rice.
Fleet electrification (EVs), modal shift from road/air to electrified rail, Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF).
Heat pumps, building envelope insulation, LED retrofits, passive solar design.

sections.heading: 4. Key Mitigation Technologies
sections.content:
• Energy Efficiency: Designated by the IEA as the 'first fuel' — cleanest and cheapest decarbonization mechanism.
• Carbon Capture & Storage (CCS): Capturing industrial flue gas CO2 and sequestering it securely deep underground in saline aquifers or depleted oil fields.
• Carbon Capture & Utilisation (CCU): Transforming captured CO2 into commercial building aggregates, synthetic fuels, or chemicals.
• Direct Air Capture (DAC): Scrubbing dilute CO2 directly from ambient air using chemical contactors.
• Carbon Offsets: High-integrity credits must satisfy 4 criteria: Additional (would not happen without finance), Measurable, Permanent (non-reversal), and Independently Verified.

fatNotes.title: Solar & Wind Energy (W6S1 Part 1)
fatNotes.intro: Engineering principles of photovoltaic cells, Concentrated Solar Power (CSP), wind turbine mechanics, HAWT vs VAWT, Betz limit, and Indian renewable policies.

sections.heading: 1. Solar Photovoltaic (PV) Technology
sections.content:
• Photovoltaic Effect: Incident photons knock valence electrons loose in a semiconductor (crystalline silicon); an internal electric field at the p-n junction sweeps free electrons, generating direct current (DC).
• Core Components: Solar PV array, Inverter (converts DC into grid-synchronized AC), Charge controller, Battery storage (optional), Mounting racks/trackers.
• Solar Output Equation: Power (W) = Irradiance (W/m²) × Panel Area (m²) × Module Efficiency (η).
• Temperature Coefficient: Solar PV efficiency decreases as temperature rises (negative coefficient, typically -0.35% to -0.45% per °C above 25 °C).

sections.heading: 2. PV Cell Types Comparison
tableRows: Single continuous crystal (Czochralski process); highest commercial efficiency; uniform dark black appearance; higher cost.
Multiple silicon fragments melted together; blue speckled look; lower manufacturing cost; grain boundaries slightly reduce efficiency.
Semiconductor deposited in microscopic layers on glass/metal; flexible, lightweight, excellent low-light response; requires larger land area.
Tandem layer on silicon tuning solar absorption bands; low production cost; currently hindered by moisture/UV degradation.

sections.heading: 3. Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) & Key Indian Schemes
sections.content:
• Concentrated Solar Power (CSP): Utilizes tracking heliostat mirrors to focus sunlight onto a central receiver tower, heating molten salt to >550 °C to generate superheated steam for conventional turbines with dispatchable thermal energy storage.
• Key Indian Solar Schemes:
- PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana: Rooftop solar for 1 crore households with subsidies up to ₹78,000.
- PM-KUSUM: Solarization of agricultural pump sets (up to 60% subsidy to replace diesel pumps).
- Bhadla Solar Park (Rajasthan): World's largest operational solar park (~2,245 MW).
- International Solar Alliance (ISA): Co-founded by India and France; headquarters in Gurugram, India.

sections.heading: 4. Wind Turbine Mechanics & Betz Limit
sections.content:
• Wind Power Physics: Kinetic energy of moving air converted to electricity. Power Equation: P = 0.5 × ρ × A × v³ (Power is proportional to the cube of wind speed — doubling wind speed yields 8x power).
• Betz Limit: Theoretical aerodynamic ceiling proving no wind turbine can extract more than 59.3% (16/27) of kinetic energy from wind.
• Turbine Speeds: Cut-in speed (3–4 m/s, blades begin rotating); Rated wind speed (12–15 m/s, maximum generator output); Cut-out speed (~25 m/s, pitch brakes activate to prevent mechanical failure).
• HAWT vs VAWT: Horizontal Axis Wind Turbines (HAWT) dominate commercial power due to superior aerodynamic efficiency; Vertical Axis Wind Turbines (VAWT) accept wind from any direction, ideal for turbulent urban settings.
• Indian Geography: Western coast (Gujarat, Maharashtra) is preferred due to consistent winds; Eastern coast is cyclone-prone. National Institute of Wind Energy (NIWE) is headquartered in Chennai. Muppandal Wind Farm (Tamil Nadu) is one of the world's largest.

fatNotes.title: Hydroelectric & Geothermal Energy (W6S1 Part 2)
fatNotes.intro: Hydraulic head and penstocks, pumped storage, dam impacts, geothermal enthalpy classification, flash vs binary plants, and tectonic sites.

sections.heading: 1. Hydroelectric Power Generation
sections.content:
• Energy Conversion Chain: Potential Energy (water head in reservoir) -> Kinetic Energy (rushing through penstock) -> Mechanical Energy (turbine rotation) -> Electrical Energy (generator).
• Power Equation: P = ρ × g × Q × H × η (where ρ = water density, g = 9.81 m/s², Q = volumetric discharge in m³/s, H = effective hydraulic head in metres, η = turbine-generator efficiency >90%).
• Hydropower Classifications:
- Storage / Impoundment: Large dam reservoir storing seasonal discharge (e.g., Tehri Dam, 1000 MW, Uttarakhand - highest in India).
- Run-of-the-River: Diverts natural river flow through tunnels/canals with minimal reservoir flooding (e.g., Srinagar Hydro, 330 MW, Alaknanda).
- Pumped Storage Hydro (PSH): Acts as a giant rechargeable grid battery; pumps water uphill during off-peak hours and discharges downhill during peak demand (e.g., Kadamparai, 400 MW, Tamil Nadu).
• Environmental Trade-offs: Zero direct operating stack emissions, but decaying submerged biomass in tropical reservoirs emits biogenic methane (CH4); blocks fish migration; causes reservoir-induced seismicity and downstream silt deprivation.

sections.heading: 2. Geothermal Energy & Plant Architectures
sections.content:
• Geothermal Gradient: Normal continental temperature rise of 25–30 °C per kilometre of depth into Earth's crust.
• Geothermal Plant Thermodynamic Cycles:
- Dry Steam Plants: Directly exploits rare natural dry underground steam (>200 °C) to drive turbines (e.g., The Geysers, California).
- Flash Steam Plants: High-pressure deep water (>180 °C) is sprayed into lower-pressure flash tanks, instantaneously boiling ('flashing') into steam. Most prevalent global technology.
- Binary Cycle Plants: Utilizes moderate geothermal fluid temperatures (100–180 °C) to heat a secondary organic working fluid with a lower boiling point (isobutane or pentane) in a closed heat exchanger. Geothermal water is 100% re-injected without atmospheric release.
• Indian Geothermal Prospects: Puga Valley (Ladakh - highest enthalpy in India), Tattapani (Chhattisgarh), Manikaran (Himachal Pradesh), Cambay Basin (Gujarat).

fatNotes.title: AI & IoT in Environmental Monitoring
fatNotes.intro: Sensors (NPK, optical dust, gas arrays), telemetry protocols, edge AI, LSTM pollution forecasting, digital twins, and case studies.

sections.heading: 1. IoT Sensor Matrix for Environmental Telemetry
tableRows: Optical light scattering, MQ-135, electrochemical sensors
PM2.5, PM10, CO, SO2, NOx, ground-level O3, volatile organic compounds (VOCs)
Ion-selective electrodes, optical dissolved oxygen probes, turbidity meters
pH, Dissolved Oxygen (DO), Electrical Conductivity (EC), Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD), turbidity
Volumetric soil moisture, soil temperature, Nitrogen (N), Phosphorus (P), Potassium (K) levels
Bioacoustic microphones, PIR motion camera traps
Ultrasonic bat calls, illegal chain-saw logging sounds, wildlife poaching identification
Ultrasonic level sensors inside smart dumpsters
Trash bin fill percentage, automated route optimization for municipal compactor trucks

sections.heading: 2. Artificial Intelligence in Environmental Protection
sections.content:
• Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) Networks: Recurrent neural networks ideal for processing temporal atmospheric time-series data to forecast air quality (AQI) 24–72 hours in advance.
• Digital Twins: Real-time physics-grounded 3D computational replicas of water treatment plants, urban airsheds, or river basins continuously updated by IoT telemetry to simulate failure scenarios.
• Computer Vision: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) analyzing multi-spectral drone and satellite imagery to calculate NDVI (vegetation index) and map illegal deforestation.
• Landmark Indian AI Case Study: IIT Kharagpur researchers developed an AI geospatial machine learning framework predicting high-risk arsenic contamination in groundwater across the Ganga delta.

fatNotes.title: Last-Minute Exam Tips & VIT Marking Guide
fatNotes.intro: High-frequency 2-mark definitions, 5/10-mark structures, and examiners' preferred keywords.
bullets: Frequent 2-Mark Definitions to Memorise verbatim: Carbon footprint (CO2e), Global Warming Potential (GWP100), Scope 1 vs Scope 2 vs Scope 3, Betz limit (59.3%), Photovoltaic effect (p-n junction), Flash vs Binary geothermal cycles, Run-of-river vs Pumped storage hydro, Digital Twin.
Frequent 5/10-Mark Question Frameworks: When asked for working principles of Solar PV / Wind / Hydro / Geothermal, ALWAYS draw the labelled block diagram showing the energy conversion chain.
Always include Indian context: Mention 500 GW by 2030, Net-Zero 2070, PM Surya Ghar, Bhadla Solar Park (Rajasthan), Muppandal (Tamil Nadu), Tehri Dam (Uttarakhand), Puga Valley (Ladakh).
Marking Scheme Tip: VIT examiners heavily reward technical terms (Clausius-Clapeyron, calcination, Betz limit, isobutane, enthalpy, LSTM, ISO 14064, CPCB under Water Act 1974).

masterdooomTopics.title: Earth as a Life Support System
masterdooomTopics.sub: Four Earth spheres + atmosphere layers + water/geosphere/biosphere basics
must: Earth’s four major spheres: lithosphere (rock/minerals), hydrosphere (water), biosphere (life), atmosphere (air/weather).
Atmosphere is the gaseous envelope; mainly 78% N₂ and 21% O₂.
Atmospheric layers from ground upward: Troposphere → Stratosphere → Mesosphere → Thermosphere → Exosphere.
Troposphere: weather + most atmospheric mass; temperature generally decreases with altitude.
Stratosphere: ozone layer; absorbs harmful UV; temperature rises with altitude.
Mesosphere: coldest layer; meteors burn up here.
Thermosphere: temperature rises; absorbs energetic UV/X-rays; auroras occur here.
Exosphere: outermost layer, gradually merging/leaking into space.
Earth functions as an interconnected system: changes in one sphere can affect the others, such as rainfall influencing soil, rivers and living organisms.
The atmosphere regulates temperature, supports weather and climate, and provides gases needed for life.
The hydrosphere includes oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater, glaciers and atmospheric water; most of Earth’s water is saline.
The lithosphere provides soil, minerals and the physical base for terrestrial ecosystems.
The biosphere interacts with the other spheres through processes such as photosynthesis, decomposition and nutrient cycling.

masterdooomTopics.title: Ecosystem — Core Concepts
masterdooomTopics.sub: Ecology, levels of organization, natural vs artificial ecosystems
must: Ecology = study of organisms in their natural home interacting with surroundings.
Ecosystem = biotic communities interacting with the non-living environment, exchanging energy and matter.
Ecological organization: Organism → Population → Community → Ecosystem → Biosphere.
Population = same species in an area. Community = multiple populations in an area.
Biosphere = sum/global ecological system of all ecosystems on Earth.
Natural ecosystems evolve without human intervention; artificial ecosystems require management.
An ecosystem has two broad components: biotic organisms and the abiotic environment they interact with.
Ecosystems can be small, such as a pond, or large, such as a forest or ocean.
Energy enters an ecosystem and moves through feeding relationships, while materials are continuously recycled.
Habitat is the place where an organism lives; its ecological role or function is its niche.
Examples of artificial ecosystems include crop fields, aquariums and managed gardens.

masterdooomTopics.title: Ecosystem Structure & Functions
masterdooomTopics.sub: Biotic/abiotic components, ecosystem types, trophic levels, nutrient cycling
must: Biotic = living components: producers, consumers, decomposers. Abiotic = physical/chemical factors: light, temperature, water, soil, air, minerals, pH, salinity.
Producers form the base by converting solar energy to chemical energy.
Consumers include herbivores, carnivores, omnivores and parasites.
Decomposers such as bacteria/fungi break down dead organisms and recycle nutrients.
Trophic levels: producers → primary consumers → secondary consumers → tertiary consumers.
About 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level; ~90% is lost mainly as heat.
Food chain is linear; food web is interconnected and more realistic.
Major nutrient cycles in the notes include water, carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus cycles.
Producers are autotrophs that manufacture organic food; consumers obtain energy by feeding on other organisms.
Decomposers return simpler nutrients to the environment, making them available again to producers.
Abiotic factors influence productivity and distribution of organisms; examples include light, temperature, water and soil conditions.
Food chains show one pathway of energy transfer, while food webs connect many feeding pathways.
Ecological pyramids can represent numbers, biomass or energy; the energy pyramid is always upright.

masterdooomTopics.title: Energy Flow in an Ecosystem
masterdooomTopics.sub: Photosynthesis, GPP/NPP, food chains, pyramids and thermodynamics
must: All ecosystem energy enters mainly through producers via photosynthesis; deep-sea chemoautotrophs use chemical energy.
Photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
GPP = total energy fixed by photosynthesis. Respiration = energy used by producer. NPP = GPP − respiration.
NPP is the energy available to the rest of the food chain.
Grazing food chain starts with living green plants; detritus food chain starts with dead organic matter.
Food webs provide alternate feeding pathways and can increase ecosystem stability.
Energy pyramid is ALWAYS upright because energy decreases at successive trophic levels.
First law: energy is conserved during transformations. Second law: transformations release heat, explaining one-way energy flow.
Only a fraction of incoming solar radiation is captured by producers, and only part of that captured energy becomes biomass available to consumers.
Gross Primary Productivity measures total photosynthetic production, while Net Primary Productivity represents production remaining after plant respiration.
As energy moves between trophic levels, much is used for metabolism and released as heat, so higher trophic levels receive less usable energy.
Detritivores and decomposers process dead organic matter and connect the detritus pathway with nutrient cycling.
Food webs are generally more stable than a single food chain because organisms may have alternative food sources.

masterdooomTopics.title: Ecological Succession
masterdooomTopics.sub: Primary/secondary succession, stages, pioneer and climax communities
must: Ecological succession = gradual change in species composition and community processes over time.
Primary succession begins on barren/lifeless substrate; soil formation starts with pioneer species such as lichens and mosses.
Secondary succession occurs where a previous ecosystem was disturbed but soil/life remnants remain.
Secondary succession is much faster because soil and nutrients remain; the notes state roughly 5–10× faster.
Sequence: Nudation → Invasion → Competition → Climax/stabilization.
Pioneers arrive first and modify the environment; climax community is the relatively stable end stage.
Hydrosere starts in water; xerosere in dry habitat; lithosere on rocks; halosere in saline habitat.
Monoclimax theory: F.E. Clements; polyclimax theory: A.G. Tansley.
Nudation creates or exposes a bare area; invasion introduces pioneer organisms that can survive the initial conditions.
Pioneers alter the environment by adding organic matter and helping create conditions for later species.
During competition and replacement, species better suited to the changing environment become established.
Primary succession is slow because soil must develop; secondary succession starts with an existing soil layer.
A climax community represents a relatively stable stage under the prevailing environmental conditions.

masterdooomTopics.title: Biodiversity — Definition & Levels
masterdooomTopics.sub: Genetic, species and ecosystem diversity + significance
must: Biodiversity = variety of life, including genes, species and ecosystems.
Genetic diversity = variation in genes/traits within one species. Example: rice varieties or dog breeds.
Species diversity = number and types of species in an area; includes species richness and evenness.
Ecosystem diversity = variety of ecosystems/habitats and their processes.
Higher biodiversity supports resilience, ecological stability, food security, health and livelihoods.
Economic value includes agriculture, pharmaceuticals, bioproducts and ecotourism.
Forests act as carbon sinks; wetlands help filter water and reduce floods.
Genetic diversity gives populations variation that can help them adapt to environmental change, pests and disease.
Species richness measures how many species are present, while evenness describes how equally individuals are distributed among those species.
Ecosystem diversity includes variation among habitats such as forests, wetlands, grasslands and aquatic systems.
Biodiversity has ecological, economic, cultural, aesthetic and scientific value.
Loss of biodiversity can weaken ecosystem functions and reduce resilience to environmental disturbances.

masterdooomTopics.title: Species Interactions & Species Status
masterdooomTopics.sub: Mutualism, commensalism, parasitism, predation, competition + extinction categories
must: Mutualism (+,+): both benefit. Example: bees and flowering plants.
Commensalism (+,0): one benefits, other is unaffected. Example: barnacles on whales.
Parasitism (+,−): parasite benefits, host is harmed. Example: ticks on mammals.
Predation (+,−): predator kills/consumes prey.
Competition (−,−): organisms compete for limited resources; both incur a cost.
Extinct = no living individuals remain. Endangered = at high risk of extinction. Endemic = naturally restricted to a particular geographic area. Rare = occurs in small numbers/limited populations.
Mutualism can be obligate or facultative, but the defining feature is that both interacting species gain a benefit.
In commensalism, one species gains while the other experiences no significant benefit or harm.
Parasitism differs from predation because the parasite generally lives on or in the host and does not normally kill it immediately.
Competition becomes stronger when species depend on the same limited resource such as food, water, space or light.
Endemic species may have very small geographic ranges, which can make habitat disturbance especially important for their conservation.

masterdooomTopics.title: Conservation Strategies
masterdooomTopics.sub: Why conserve + in-situ/ex-situ approaches + protected areas
must: Conservation aims to protect biodiversity while allowing sustainable use of biological resources.
In-situ conservation = conserving species in their natural habitat. Examples: national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves.
Ex-situ conservation = conserving outside the natural habitat. Examples: zoos, botanical gardens, seed/gene banks, captive breeding.
Genetic diversity is important for adaptation and disease/pest resistance.
Habitat protection is central because species interactions and ecological processes depend on functioning ecosystems.
Conservation supports ecosystem services such as pollination, water filtration and climate regulation.
In-situ conservation protects organisms together with the habitat and ecological relationships they depend on.
Ex-situ conservation is useful when a species is severely threatened or when controlled breeding and genetic storage are needed.
Protected areas can reduce habitat destruction, hunting and other pressures, but effective management is still required.
Seed banks and gene banks preserve genetic material that can support future research, breeding and restoration.
Conservation is most effective when ecological, genetic and human resource-use considerations are considered together.

masterdooomTopics.title: Genetically Modified (GM) Crops
masterdooomTopics.sub: Definition, genetic engineering, benefits, risks and examples
must: GM crops have DNA altered using genetic engineering to introduce desirable traits.
Genes can be transferred with high precision, including between unrelated species.
Common goals: higher yield, pest/disease resistance, drought/salinity/temperature tolerance, improved food security.
Basic process: identify useful gene → isolate → insert into plant DNA → express desired trait → select/propagate.
Potential benefits in the notes: reduced crop losses and potentially reduced chemical inputs.
Key concern areas: ecological effects, gene flow, resistance development, biosafety and socio-economic questions.
Genetic engineering can introduce, remove or modify specific genetic material to produce a desired characteristic.
Bt crops are an example discussed in environmental science because they use a gene associated with resistance to certain insect pests.
Possible agricultural benefits include reduced crop losses and improved tolerance to environmental stresses.
Potential concerns include unintended ecological effects, gene flow to related plants and evolution of resistant pests.
Assessment of GM crops involves biosafety, environmental monitoring, food safety and socio-economic considerations.

masterdooomTopics.title: Air Pollution
masterdooomTopics.sub: Primary/secondary pollutants, AQI, smog, acid rain and health effects
must: Air pollution = harmful substances in the atmosphere at concentrations capable of causing damage.
Clean-air composition in the notes: ~78% N₂, ~21% O₂, remaining trace gases.
Primary pollutants are emitted directly: CO, SO₂, NOₓ, PM, VOCs, NH₃, Pb.
Secondary pollutants form by atmospheric reactions: ground-level O₃, PAN, sulfuric/nitric acids and secondary PM.
Photochemical smog: NOₓ + VOCs + sunlight → ground-level O₃/PAN.
SO₂ and NOₓ contribute to acid rain. PM2.5 can penetrate deeply into lungs.
AQI in the supplied notes: 0–50 good; 51–100 acceptable; 101–200 unhealthy; 201–300 unhealthy; 301–400 very unhealthy; 401–500 hazardous.
Particulate matter is classified by particle size; PM2.5 is small enough to penetrate deeply into the respiratory system.
Carbon monoxide reduces the blood’s oxygen-carrying capacity by binding strongly with haemoglobin.
Ground-level ozone is formed secondarily and is a major component of photochemical smog.
Acid deposition forms when sulfur and nitrogen oxides undergo atmospheric reactions and produce acidic compounds.
Air-pollution control can target the source, for example cleaner fuels, emission controls, public transport and industrial treatment systems.

masterdooomTopics.title: Water Pollution
masterdooomTopics.sub: Sources, BOD/COD, eutrophication, biomagnification and treatment
must: Water pollution = physical, chemical or biological contamination that degrades water quality and makes it unfit for intended use.
Point source = identifiable single discharge point, e.g. factory pipe. Non-point source = diffuse runoff, e.g. agricultural runoff.
Groundwater pollution can occur when pesticides, industrial chemicals or heavy metals seep through soil into aquifers.
BOD = oxygen required by microorganisms to biologically break down biodegradable organic matter. Higher BOD generally indicates greater organic pollution.
Eutrophication = nutrient enrichment → algal growth → decomposition → oxygen depletion → aquatic stress/death.
Biomagnification = persistent pollutants become more concentrated at higher trophic levels.
Wastewater treatment: Primary physical → Secondary biological → Tertiary advanced/disinfection.
Nature-based solutions in the notes include phytoremediation, bioremediation, riparian buffers and wetland restoration.
DO (dissolved oxygen) is important for aquatic organisms; pollution that increases oxygen demand can reduce available DO.
BOD is commonly used as an indicator of biodegradable organic load, whereas COD represents oxygen needed for chemical oxidation of oxidizable matter.
Eutrophication is strongly associated with excess nitrogen and phosphorus entering water bodies.
Primary treatment mainly removes physical solids, secondary treatment uses biological processes, and tertiary treatment targets remaining nutrients, chemicals or pathogens.
Persistent pollutants can move through food webs, causing higher concentrations in organisms at higher trophic levels.

masterdooomTopics.title: Soil Pollution
masterdooomTopics.sub: Definition, pollutants, sources, impacts and control
must: Soil pollution/contamination involves xenobiotic (human-made) chemicals or other harmful alteration of natural soil.
Major sources: industrial activity, agricultural chemicals, improper waste disposal, urbanization and deforestation.
Pollutants include heavy metals, inorganic salts, pesticides, hydrocarbons/PAHs and other organic compounds.
Risks occur through direct soil contact, vapours and secondary contamination of groundwater/water supplies.
Excess fertilizer/pesticide use can contaminate soil and water; poor irrigation can cause salinization and waterlogging.
Control focuses on proper waste management, reduced chemical inputs, remediation and sustainable land use.
Soil contaminants can change soil properties, reduce fertility and affect soil organisms.
Heavy metals such as lead, cadmium and mercury can persist because they do not readily biodegrade.
Pesticides may move from soil into plants, groundwater or surface water depending on their properties and environmental conditions.
Phytoremediation uses plants to remove, stabilize or transform contaminants in affected soil.
Prevention is generally preferable to remediation because contaminated soil can be difficult and expensive to restore.

masterdooomTopics.title: Noise Pollution
masterdooomTopics.sub: Decibels, sources, health effects and control
must: Noise pollution = unwanted/unpleasant sound that interferes with life and can harm health.
Sound is measured in decibels (dB). The notes give ~30 dB whisper, ~50 dB conversation, ~85–90 dB traffic, >120 dB concerts/firecrackers.
Prolonged exposure above ~85 dB can damage hearing; >120 dB can cause immediate harm.
Major sources: industry, transportation, construction, urbanization, loudspeakers and poorly maintained machinery.
Effects include hearing impairment, sleep disturbance, stress and cardiovascular impacts.
Control: source maintenance, barriers, zoning, silencers, PPE and limiting exposure.
Decibel is a logarithmic unit, so an increase in sound level represents a substantial change in sound intensity.
Long-term high exposure can damage the sensory structures involved in hearing.
Noise can also affect sleep, concentration, communication and stress levels even without causing immediate hearing loss.
Control measures follow the source–path–receiver approach: reduce noise at the source, block transmission, or protect the receiver.
Urban planning, traffic management and zoning can reduce population exposure to persistent noise.

masterdooomTopics.title: Thermal Pollution
masterdooomTopics.sub: Heat contamination, dissolved oxygen, causes, impacts and control
must: Thermal pollution = human-caused sudden increase/decrease in natural water temperature that alters aquatic ecosystems.
Major sources: industrial cooling water, thermal/nuclear power plants, dams/reservoirs, deforestation and warm sewage discharges.
Higher temperature reduces dissolved oxygen solubility, stressing aquatic life.
Impacts: oxygen depletion, altered metabolism/reproduction, fish mortality, invasive species, eutrophication and fisheries impacts.
Controls: cooling ponds, cooling towers, spray ponds, artificial lakes, recycling heated water and closed-loop cooling.
Temperature affects dissolved oxygen, metabolic rate and the activity of aquatic organisms.
Sudden temperature changes can create thermal shock and disrupt organisms adapted to a narrower temperature range.
Warm effluents can alter species composition and favour organisms that tolerate higher temperatures.
Cooling systems allow industries to remove heat before water is discharged or to reuse cooling water.
Maintaining natural riparian vegetation can also help moderate stream temperatures by providing shade.

masterdooomTopics.title: Water Management & Conservation
masterdooomTopics.sub: Scarcity, IWRM, rainwater harvesting, reuse and efficient irrigation
must: Water management = planning, developing, distributing and managing optimum use of water resources.
Water conservation = careful and efficient use to reduce wastage and preserve water for future needs.
Key principles: sustainability, equity, efficiency and Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM).
IWRM coordinates water, land and related resources while balancing social, economic and environmental needs.
Practical methods: rainwater harvesting, wastewater reuse/recycling, drip/micro-irrigation, leak control, efficient fixtures, industrial recycling and watershed protection.
Indian measures in the notes: National Water Policy, Jal Shakti Abhiyan, MGNREGA watershed works and PMKSY (“Per Drop More Crop”).
Water scarcity can result from limited supply, uneven distribution, over-extraction, pollution or inefficient use.
Rainwater harvesting captures rainfall for storage or groundwater recharge and reduces dependence on conventional supplies.
Drip irrigation delivers water near plant roots and can reduce losses from evaporation and runoff.
Wastewater reuse reduces demand for freshwater when the water is treated to a suitable quality.
Watershed management links soil, vegetation, drainage and water conservation across an entire drainage area.

masterdooomTopics.title: Circular Economy & Solid Waste
masterdooomTopics.sub: Linear vs circular economy, 3Rs and treatment methods
must: Solid waste = discarded solid/semi-solid material.
Waste categories: municipal, industrial, biomedical, e-waste, construction/demolition and agricultural.
Linear economy: take → make → use → dispose. Circular economy: keep materials/resources in loops for longer.
3R priority: Reduce → Reuse → Recycle.
Composting = controlled biological breakdown of organic waste with oxygen, producing nutrient-rich compost.
Anaerobic digestion = decomposition without oxygen; produces biogas (mainly methane) + digestate.
Incineration = controlled high-temperature burning; course notes give ~800–1000°C and up to ~90% volume reduction.
Sanitary landfill = engineered landfill with liners to reduce leachate contamination; landfill gas can be captured.
Integrated Solid Waste Management hierarchy in the notes: prevent → reuse → recycle → compost/digest → energy recovery → landfill last.
A circular economy aims to maintain the value of products and materials instead of treating them as disposable after one use.
Reduce prevents waste at the source; reuse extends product life; recycling recovers material for new products.
Composting is particularly suitable for biodegradable organic waste such as food and garden residues.
Anaerobic digestion can recover energy as biogas while leaving digestate that can be managed as a useful by-product.
Poorly managed waste can create leachate, air pollution, odour, disease-vector problems and greenhouse-gas emissions.

masterdooomTopics.title: Environmental Hazards
masterdooomTopics.sub: Natural/anthropogenic + physical/chemical/biological/sociological
must: Environmental hazard = natural or human-made event/condition with potential to harm health, ecosystems, property or environment.
Two broad origins: natural and anthropogenic (human-induced).
Four major types in the notes: physical, chemical, biological and sociological.
Physical: earthquakes, floods, landslides, radiation, extreme temperature, noise.
Chemical: heavy metals, pesticides, BPA, phthalates, dyes, solvents and industrial pollutants.
Biological: bacteria, viruses, parasites, fungi, prions and biological toxins.
Sociological: poverty, malnutrition, unsafe work conditions, lack of healthcare, inequality and conflict.
Risk depends on hazard magnitude and vulnerability/exposure.
A hazard becomes a risk when people, ecosystems or assets are exposed and are vulnerable to its effects.
Natural hazards include events such as floods, earthquakes and cyclones, while anthropogenic hazards arise from human activities.
Chemical hazards may enter the body through inhalation, ingestion, skin contact or other exposure routes.
Biological hazards include infectious organisms and biological toxins that can affect humans or ecosystems.
Risk reduction combines prevention, preparedness, mitigation, monitoring and emergency response.

masterdooomTopics.title: Chemical Hazards — BPA & Mercury
masterdooomTopics.sub: Endocrine disruption, heavy metals, exposure routes
must: Chemical hazard = substance/agent with potential to cause harm to health or life.
BPA is used mainly in polycarbonate plastics and epoxy resins; it can interact with estrogen receptors and act as an endocrine-disrupting chemical.
BPA-associated concerns in the notes include reproductive, neurological, metabolic and developmental effects.
Mercury is a heavy metal; methylmercury is especially important in aquatic food chains and can biomagnify.
Exposure routes: inhalation, ingestion, dermal contact, ocular exposure and transplacental exposure.
Mechanisms of chemical harm: endocrine disruption, carcinogenesis, neurotoxicity, organ toxicity, reproductive toxicity and immunotoxicity.
BPA is associated with endocrine activity because it can interact with hormone-related biological pathways.
Mercury can be released through industrial activities and can enter aquatic systems where microorganisms can convert it to methylmercury.
Methylmercury can accumulate in organisms and become more concentrated at higher trophic levels.
Exposure and toxicity depend on the chemical form, dose, duration, route of exposure and susceptibility of the organism.
Reducing exposure requires source control, safe handling, monitoring and proper management of contaminated materials.

masterdooomTopics.title: Disaster Management
masterdooomTopics.sub: Prevention, preparedness, response, recovery + floods, cyclones, earthquakes, landslides
must: Disaster management aims to minimize disaster impacts through planning and coordinated action.
Core cycle: Prevention/Mitigation → Preparedness → Response → Recovery/Rehabilitation.
Flood types in the notes: riverine, flash, coastal and urban.
Flood triggers: heavy rainfall, dam failure, storm surge, climate change, deforestation and poor urban drainage.
Landslide triggers: heavy rainfall, earthquakes, deforestation, mining/excavation, volcanic activity and construction.
Mitigation examples: drainage control, slope stabilization, afforestation, land-use planning, barriers, early warning systems.
Response = immediate evacuation, first aid, firefighting and rescue; recovery = rebuilding and restoring services.
Disaster categories in the notes also include meteorological, geological, biological, climatological and extraterrestrial disasters.
Mitigation reduces the severity or probability of disaster impacts before an event, while preparedness builds the ability to respond.
Early warning systems help communities act before hazards produce their full impacts.
Flood mitigation can include drainage improvement, floodplain management, embankments, watershed protection and warning systems.
Earthquake preparedness includes safer construction, structural strengthening, drills and emergency planning.
Recovery includes restoring infrastructure and services, supporting affected communities and reducing future vulnerability.

masterdooomTopics.title: Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA)
masterdooomTopics.sub: Screening → scoping → impact assessment → mitigation → EMP → consultation → decision → monitoring
must: EIA = process of evaluating potential environmental consequences of a proposed project before it begins.
Goals: identify/predict impacts, evaluate alternatives, develop mitigation, inform decision-makers/public and promote sustainable development.
Screening determines whether a full EIA is required and the level of assessment.
Scoping identifies key issues, defines boundaries and develops Terms of Reference (ToR).
Impact assessment forecasts positive/negative, direct/indirect, short/long-term and reversible/irreversible impacts.
Mitigation reduces or eliminates negative impacts; EMP = Environmental Management Plan.
Public consultation, review/decision and monitoring/evaluation are later stages.
Tools include checklists, matrices such as Leopold matrix, modelling, GIS and risk assessment.
Screening decides whether a project requires assessment; scoping focuses the assessment on the important environmental issues.
An EIA considers alternatives so that environmental effects are considered alongside project design and decision-making.
An Environmental Management Plan translates identified mitigation measures into actions, responsibilities and monitoring.
Public consultation provides an opportunity for affected people and stakeholders to raise environmental concerns.
Post-project monitoring checks whether predicted impacts and mitigation measures match what occurs in practice.

masterdooomTopics.title: Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
masterdooomTopics.sub: CPCB/SPCB, consent mechanism and key sections
must: First comprehensive water pollution law in independent India; enacted 23 March 1974.
Constitutional basis: Article 252, allowing Parliament to legislate on a state subject when states request it.
Established CPCB (Section 3) and SPCBs (Section 4).
Section 24: prohibition on pollution of streams/wells by disposal of poisonous/noxious/polluting matter.
Section 25: restrictions/consent mechanism for new outlets and new discharges. Section 26 deals with existing discharges.
Section 27: revocation/variation of consent. Section 32: emergency measures.
Penalty provisions are serious; the supplied notes state imprisonment from about 1.5 to 6 years plus fines for serious violations, with additional penalties for continuing offences.
The Act focuses on preventing and controlling water pollution and maintaining or restoring the wholesomeness of water.
CPCB coordinates pollution-control activities at the national level, while SPCBs operate at the state level.
Consent requirements allow pollution-control boards to regulate establishments that discharge effluents.
Section 24 is a key prohibition concerning pollution of streams and wells by poisonous, noxious or polluting matter.
Sections 25 and 26 address restrictions and consent requirements concerning new and existing discharges.

masterdooomTopics.title: Environment Protection Act, 1986 + Air Act, 1981
masterdooomTopics.sub: Umbrella environmental law + air pollution control framework
must: Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 is described in the notes as a backbone/umbrella law for environmental governance.
EPA Section 3: powers of Central Government; Section 6: environmental standards/rules; Section 7: prohibition on excess discharge; Section 8: hazardous substances; Section 10: entry/inspection.
Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981; amended in 1987, with noise added as an air pollutant in the supplied notes.
Air Act Section 19: air pollution control areas. Section 21: consent mechanism. Section 24: power to take air samples. Section 31A: directions/emergency closure powers.
CPCB and SPCBs administer major parts of the air/water pollution control framework.
Article 21 has been interpreted to include a right to a clean/healthy environment.
The Environment Protection Act followed the 1984 Bhopal gas disaster and strengthened the central framework for environmental protection.
Under the EPA, the Central Government can take measures and frame rules or standards for environmental protection.
The Air Act establishes a framework for prevention, control and abatement of air pollution.
Air pollution control areas and consent requirements allow regulatory authorities to target areas and industrial activities needing control.
Remember the sequence: Water Act 1974 → Air Act 1981 → Environment Protection Act 1986.

masterdooomTopics.title: Forest Conservation Act, 1980 + Wildlife Protection Act, 1972
masterdooomTopics.sub: Habitat protection + wildlife protection, schedules, CITES
must: Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980: restricts diversion of forest land for non-forest use.
Section 2 is the key provision: prior Central Government approval is required for specified non-forest use of forest land.
Compensatory afforestation and CAMPA funding are associated with approved diversion.
Godavarman judgment (1996) expanded application to lands that are forests in the dictionary sense, as described in the notes.
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 focuses on protecting wild animals/plants and habitats; schedules provide different levels of protection.
National Board for Wildlife is highlighted in the notes and is chaired by the Prime Minister.
CITES = Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora; regulates international wildlife trade.
The Forest Conservation Act aims to control diversion of forest land for non-forest purposes.
Prior Central Government approval is required for specified proposals involving diversion of forest land.
Compensatory afforestation is intended to address loss of forest area associated with approved diversion.
The Wildlife Protection Act provides legal protection for wild animals, plants and habitats through protected areas and schedules.
CITES works internationally by regulating trade in listed species and their specimens.

masterdooomTopics.title: Kyoto Protocol, 1997
masterdooomTopics.sub: UNFCCC → Kyoto → binding targets for developed countries + flexible mechanisms
must: Adopted in 1997 at COP3 in Kyoto.
Built under the UNFCCC framework; CBDR means common responsibility with differentiated responsibility.
Kyoto imposed legally binding emission reduction targets primarily on developed/Annex I countries.
Three flexible mechanisms: Emissions Trading, Joint Implementation (JI), Clean Development Mechanism (CDM).
CDM allowed Annex I countries to invest in emission-reduction projects in developing countries and receive credits.
India ratified Kyoto in August 2002 and was a Non-Annex I country without binding targets under the first commitment structure.
Kyoto influenced later climate architecture and the Paris Agreement.
Kyoto was adopted under the UNFCCC and introduced quantified emission-reduction commitments for developed countries in its commitment periods.
The principle of common but differentiated responsibilities reflects different historical contributions and capacities.
Emissions trading allows units or allowances to be traded between participating parties.
Joint Implementation allows an Annex I party to earn credits from qualifying emission-reduction projects in another Annex I country.
The Clean Development Mechanism links emission-reduction projects in developing countries with credits for participating developed countries.

masterdooomTopics.title: Paris Agreement, 2015
masterdooomTopics.sub: 1.5°C/2°C, NDCs, net-zero, adaptation, finance, stocktake
must: Adopted in 2015; entered into force in November 2016.
Temperature goal: hold warming well below 2°C and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.
NDC = Nationally Determined Contribution: each country sets its own climate targets/actions.
NDCs are submitted every five years; the notes describe a ratchet mechanism where successive NDCs should increase ambition.
Net-zero means emissions entering the atmosphere are balanced by removals; it does not mean literally zero emissions.
Adaptation is a core pillar alongside mitigation. Article 7 addresses adaptation; Article 9 addresses climate finance.
Enhanced Transparency Framework requires reporting; Global Stocktake occurs every five years to assess collective progress.
Important legal nuance from the notes: the treaty is legally binding, but individual NDC target outcomes are not legally binding in the same way; reporting/submission obligations are binding.
Paris moved climate action toward a nationally determined system in which each country communicates its own climate contribution.
Mitigation addresses the causes of climate change by reducing greenhouse-gas emissions or increasing removals.
Adaptation addresses the impacts of climate change by reducing vulnerability and improving resilience.
The Global Stocktake evaluates collective progress toward the Agreement’s goals and informs future ambition.
Climate finance supports developing countries in mitigation and adaptation, with developed countries playing an important role in the finance framework.

masterdooomTopics.title: Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
masterdooomTopics.sub: UN 2015 — 17 goals + sustainable development concept
must: Sustainable development: meeting present needs without compromising future generations’ ability to meet their own needs.
SDGs were agreed at the United Nations in New York in September 2015.
There are 17 SDGs.

High-yield environmental goals: SDG 6 water & sanitation; 7 affordable/clean energy; 11 sustainable cities; 12 responsible consumption/production; 13 climate action; 14 life below water; 15 life on land.
Other goals include poverty, hunger, health, education, gender equality, decent work, reduced inequalities, peace/justice and partnerships.
Sustainable development links economic, social and environmental dimensions rather than treating environment separately.
The 17 SDGs form an integrated framework intended to address economic, social and environmental development together.
SDG 6 focuses on clean water and sanitation, while SDG 7 focuses on affordable and clean energy.
SDG 11 addresses sustainable cities and communities; SDG 12 addresses responsible consumption and production.
SDG 13 focuses on climate action, SDG 14 on life below water, and SDG 15 on life on land.
The goals are interconnected: progress in areas such as poverty, health, education and infrastructure can influence environmental outcomes.
